extracted.intended_audience: general readers and participants (authors, publishers, judges) seeking information about the Booker Prize
extracted.subtask_description: Information and procedural standards for eligibility, submission, judging, and awarding of the Booker Prize — the annual UK/Irish literary award for sustained fiction in English. Includes rules on who may enter, how entries are submitted and considered, the judges' duties and process, and prize rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award definition / purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Awarded for 'Best work of sustained fiction of the year, written in English and published in the UK or Ireland.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the core evaluative target: a single sustained work of fiction published in the UK or Ireland and written in English; frames the prize as selecting a 'best book' annually and underpins subsequent eligibility and judging rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and publication-location eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Work must be written in English and published in the United Kingdom or Ireland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement remained central when the prize's nationality rules were widened in 2014; translations and non-English works belong to related awards (International Booker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationality / citizenship eligibility (historical and current)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally limited to citizens of the Commonwealth, Republic of Ireland and South Africa (later Zimbabwe). Since 2014 eligibility was widened to any English-language novel published in the UK or Ireland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2014 expansion to worldwide authors writing in English was controversial among some former judges and authors, and led to debate about the prize's identity and effects on diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format eligibility — 'sustained fiction' (novels vs short-story collections)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Booker Prize is for a single work of sustained fiction (generally novels); short-story collections are not generally eligible for the Booker Prize (short-story collections are eligible for the International Booker Prize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice Munro's short-story collection being shortlisted in 1980 is noted as a rare exception; format expectations affect which submissions judges will consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission rules and publisher quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: Each publisher's imprint may submit a number of titles based on their longlisting history (non-longlisted publishers one title; publishers with previous longlists can submit more, up to four for those with five or more longlisted books in the past five years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quota system (in place since 2014) determines how many entries a publisher imprint can put forward; it privileges imprints with a stronger recent Booker track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic consideration of previous winners
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous winners of the prize are automatically considered if they enter new titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previous winners do not need special nomination treatment beyond their entry, but are guaranteed consideration among submitted works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call-in / written representations for titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Books may also be 'called in': publishers can make written representations to the judges to consider titles in addition to those already entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a procedural route for publishers to ask judges to consider works that might otherwise be omitted from submissions; used to expand the pool beyond standard entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longlist publication and size ('Booker Dozen')
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges select a longlist of 12 or 13 titles (the 'Booker Dozen'); from 2001 the longlist has been publicly revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The longlist is the first public selection stage; the number is capped and has been standardized since 2007 at 12 or 13 in many years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortlist size
rubrics_metrics.description: From the longlist judges select a shortlist of six titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shortlist is the second public stage before the final winner announcement; shortlisted authors each receive a monetary award and a specially bound edition of their book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging panel composition and appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: A five-person panel is appointed each year by the Booker Prize Foundation (chief executive in consultation with an advisory committee); judges are selected from authors, publishers, journalists, literary critics, academics and public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Foundation (chief executive Gaby Wood mentioned) selects judges; panels change yearly and occasionally a judge may be selected a second time. Composition aims to include a range of literary and public perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' reading responsibilities and evaluation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Each judge is expected to read all of the books submitted. After reading all submissions they select the longlist, then read longlisted books a second time, shortlist six titles and read those a third time before selecting a winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process is intensive (judges read ~130–163 books in recent years across several months). Decisions are made by the five-person panel, with an emphasis on consensus; the procedure and heavy reading load are often cited in debates about how well a small panel can judge 'the best book.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement (rule) for a single winner
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1993 a rule was drawn up making it mandatory for the appointed jury to make the award to a single author/book (i.e., only one winner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule was established after a split award in 1992; however, in 2019 the jury breached this rule and divided the prize between two authors, demonstrating that rules can be contested by judges in exceptional circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize money and rewards for shortlisted authors
rubrics_metrics.description: The winner receives £50,000; each shortlisted author receives £2,500 and a specially bound edition of their book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize monies have changed over time (originally £5,000; raised to £50,000 in 2002). The financial and publicity benefits (sales boost) are central to the award's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and archival rules regarding judging records
rubrics_metrics.description: The Booker Prize Archive is held at Oxford Brookes University; embargoes of ten or twenty years apply to certain categories of material, including material relating to the judging process and the Longlist prior to 2002.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule governs access to administrative and judging records for historical research and transparency, with delayed release for confidentiality of the judging process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and transparency practices (longlist publicity since 2001)
rubrics_metrics.description: From 2001 the longlisted novels started to be published each year; longlist and shortlist announcements are public and generate media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public longlists increased transparency and public engagement, but also intensified media scrutiny and debate about selection criteria and perceived biases.
